final.title: What capacity limits usually hide
final.body:
Capacity limits are often not a vague “we need AI” problem. In a small business, they usually show up in one repeatable workflow decision: do you keep answering the same customer questions by hand, or do you build a bounded system for the routine part and leave judgment with you? That is the real comparison for an owner-operator: another hire, more manual work, or a narrow automation investment.

The useful diagnostic is simple. Ask whether the requests fall into a small set of common patterns, or whether each case is genuinely different. If the work is mostly repeatable, AI can help with the standard part. If each case needs live judgment, context, or a human call, then forcing automation is the wrong move. That is a boundary, not a failure.

Bareni’s next step is not to “AI everything.” It is to identify one recurring workflow, check whether it is suitable, and only then define a small pilot with clear scope, fixed price, and measures. That describes intended pilot scope, not a promise of outcomes. Human approval stays in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

That is usually what capacity limits hide: not a shortage of ambition, but a bottleneck in one boring process that keeps sitting on the desk.
